overview: This file documents a May–July 1937 complaint by the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America that Japanese postal authorities had delayed, opened, and read mail sent from the United States to the Tokyo manager of United Artists Corporation. The State Department referred the allegation to the American Consul General in Tokyo, whose investigation found the suspicion plausible but learned that the manager, A. A. Lowe, had intended only to inform his home office and did not want official action. Consular officials noted similar complaints from other Americans, including suspicions about consular mail, but believed that representations to Japanese authorities would be futile without definite proof; they also suggested that unusually large consolidated envelopes might be examined because they could be suspected of containing motion-picture films imported without censorship. The correspondence concludes with the Department reporting these findings to Frederick L. Herron and Herron apologizing for the failure of the United Artists representative to clarify or pursue his complaint.

subfiles.title: Herron complaint concerning United Artists mail in Tokyo
subfiles.from: Frederick L. Herron, Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America, Inc.
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Department of State
subfiles.about: Herron reports that Japanese authorities have allegedly delayed, opened, and read mail addressed to the United Artists manager in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Herron relays a report that the United Artists manager in Tokyo received three weeks of accumulated mail from the United States and found that all the letters had apparently been opened and read. He asks Hornbeck to involve the American Embassy in an effort to end this interference with the company's business communications.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck reply promising a consular investigation
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Hornbeck acknowledges Herron's complaint and states that the American Consul General in Tokyo will investigate it.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck notes that Herron's letter does not say whether the United Artists representative has already made local representations about the alleged tampering. He nevertheless informs Herron that the Department is instructing the American Consul General in Tokyo to investigate and take appropriate action.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Consul General Garrels to investigate
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Arthur Garrels, American Consul General in Tokyo
subfiles.about: The State Department directs Garrels to investigate the United Artists complaint and, if warranted, approach the local postal authorities.
subfiles.summary: The instruction encloses a copy of Herron's May 7 letter and describes the allegation that Japanese postal authorities were interfering with the company's mail. Garrels is ordered to establish the facts, make an appropriate local inquiry if circumstances justify it, and report his findings to the Department.

subfiles.title: Herron clarification concerning the Tokyo complaint
subfiles.about: Herron clarifies that the United Artists representative complained to the Tokyo post office but apparently did not approach the American Embassy.
subfiles.summary: Herron thanks Hornbeck for taking up the matter in Tokyo. He explains that the United Artists representative had complained directly to the Tokyo post office, although Herron does not believe that he had raised the issue with the American Embassy.

subfiles.title: Consul General Garrels's report on alleged mail tampering
subfiles.about: Garrels reports the results of his interview with A. A. Lowe and explains why the Consulate General will take no further action.
subfiles.summary: Garrels identifies A. A. Lowe as the United Artists manager concerned and reports that Lowe had not intended to make an official complaint, regretted failing to qualify his remarks to his home office, and requested that no action be taken. Garrels considers it probable that Lowe's mail had been scrutinized and notes comparable suspicions among American firms, individuals, and even consular officials, but says the Embassy judged representations futile without definite proof. Lowe explained that only large envelopes consolidating numerous letters seemed affected, leading Garrels to suggest that postal officials might suspect an attempt to import motion-picture films without censorship. The Consulate General therefore closes the matter without further action.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck reports the consular findings to Herron
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Hornbeck informs Herron that the Consulate General found insufficient evidence for official representations and that Lowe had requested no action.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck summarizes and quotes Garrels's June 17 report, noting recurrent American suspicions that mail in Japan was delayed or opened. He explains that the Embassy considered an approach to the competent authorities useless without definite proof. He also tells Herron that Lowe characterized his comments to the home office as merely informative and asked that no action be taken.

subfiles.title: Herron's acknowledgment and apology
subfiles.about: Herron thanks Hornbeck for obtaining the report and apologizes for the United Artists representative's failure to follow up his complaint.
subfiles.summary: Herron acknowledges Hornbeck's letter of July 22 and expresses appreciation for the investigation. He apologizes because the United Artists representative failed to clarify or pursue the complaint with the company's home office.

interest: The file provides a compact, complete example of how a private American business complaint moved through the State Department and the consular service in prewar Japan. Particularly revealing is the gap between officials' private belief that postal scrutiny probably occurred and their unwillingness to protest without definite evidence. The report also links postal surveillance to Japan's censorship of imported motion-picture films, suggesting why large consolidated envelopes attracted attention. Finally, Lowe's withdrawal of the complaint illustrates how commercial caution and incomplete communication could curtail diplomatic action even when officials considered the underlying allegation credible.
